name: Srisailam Mallikarjuna Temple
deity: Shiva as Mallikarjuna (a Jyotirlinga) with the goddess Bhramaramba (a Shakti Peetha)
period: Ancient shrine; developed under the Reddy and Vijayanagara kings
summary: High in the forested Nallamala hills above the Krishna river, Srisailam is rare among Indian shrines in being both a Jyotirlinga of Shiva, as Mallikarjuna, and a Shakti Peetha of the goddess, as Bhramaramba — a summit of both great streams of devotion.

sections.history: Srisailam has been sacred for well over a thousand years, praised by saints and poets and honoured in the Shaiva and Shakta scriptures alike. Set deep in the Nallamala forest above the gorge of the Krishna, its remoteness only deepened its sanctity. The fortified walls, gateways, and pillared halls that shape the temple today were largely raised under the Reddy kings and the Vijayanagara emperors, who counted Srisailam among the foremost pilgrimages of the Deccan; the great teacher Adi Shankara is traditionally said to have worshipped here.
sections.architecture: The temple stands within a large fortified enclosure whose stone walls carry long friezes of carved reliefs — processions, myths, and figures — among the finest such sculpted walls in the south. Within, the Mallikarjuna shrine holds the Jyotirlinga, and a separate shrine enshrines the goddess Bhramaramba, "she of the bees," so that Shiva and Shakti are worshipped together at one site. Gateway towers, mandapas, and later additions cluster within the walls, high above the river that has now been dammed into a great reservoir below.
sections.legends: Srisailam’s legend tells of Shiva and Parvati following their son Kartikeya, who had withdrawn in a sulk to a far hill; unable to bear the separation, the divine parents came to dwell on this mountain to be near him, taking the forms of Mallikarjuna and Bhramaramba. The name joins mallika, jasmine, with Arjuna, and the goddess Bhramaramba is remembered for taking the form of a bee, bhramara, to destroy a demon. As one of the twelve Jyotirlingas and one of the eighteen Shakti Peethas, the hill gathers two of the greatest pilgrimage traditions into a single ascent.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is Srisailam’s supreme festival, drawing immense crowds through the night, and the Brahmotsavam that surrounds it fills days with processions and temple cars. Ugadi, the Telugu new year, and the Navaratri worship of Bhramaramba are kept with special grandeur. Kumbham and Dasara bring further celebration, and pilgrims come year-round to a shrine that unites the vows of both Shaivas and devotees of the goddess.
sections.experience: The road to Srisailam winds up through the Nallamala forest, and arrival at the hilltop temple carries the sense of a hard-won pilgrimage. Within the fortified walls, the long sculpted friezes reward slow walking, relief after relief emerging in the light, before darshan of the Jyotirlinga and the goddess. The forest air, the distant gleam of the dammed Krishna, and the knowledge of standing at once in a Jyotirlinga and a Shakti Peetha give the place a rare gravity; many pilgrims complete both shrines before descending through the hills.

visit.timings: Generally open from around 4:30 am to 10:00 pm daily, with several pujas; hours extend greatly during Maha Shivaratri and Brahmotsavam.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — dhotis or trousers for men, sarees or salwar kameez for women, shoulders and knees covered; footwear is removed at the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally not permitted inside the sanctums; follow posted rules and staff guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Srisailam is in Nandyal district, about 180 km from Kurnool and 210 km from Hyderabad, reached by road through the Nallamala hills; the nearest airport is Hyderabad.
